stem: OpenAI's help page describes what ChatGPT is doing when it answers. Which of these is the vendor's own account of where a response comes from?

choices.text: It looks the answer up in a store of verified facts and reports what it finds there.
It produces responses based on patterns in the data it was trained on, and, like any language model, it can produce incorrect or misleading output.
It computes each answer step by step, so a number in a response is the result of a calculation.
It retrieves the current answer from the web for every question, so its responses are never out of date.

feedback: OpenAI's page says ChatGPT is designed to provide useful responses based on patterns in the data it was trained on, and that, like any language model, it can produce incorrect or misleading outputs. That is the whole of the vendor's account, and it is the one this lesson builds on. Choice (a) describes a lookup, which no source says the model performs. Choice (c) is the mistake section 05 exists to correct: an ordinary response is generated, not computed, and the page ties accurate calculation to a separate tool. Choice (d) is wrong on the page's own terms — without search enabled, responses are based on what the model learned during training, and the knowledge cutoff in section 03 exists precisely because responses are not drawn from the web by default. Re-read section 01.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 1 (patterns in training data; incorrect or misleading), entry 10 (without search, training only) and entry 12 (the calculation tool); guide/03/01-generated-not-computed.md, second paragraph. No flag inherited — sec-01 carries no UNSOURCED flag (drafts/GPT-01-review.md).

stem: A response from ChatGPT cites a numbered paragraph of a standard in support of a position. Which statement matches what this lesson's sources say about that citation?

choices.text: A citation that carries a paragraph number has been checked against the document and can be relied on.
It may be fabricated: OpenAI names fabricated quotes, studies, citations, or references to non-existent sources as a form of hallucination, and says to always verify references to external documents.
ChatGPT only cites documents it has retrieved, so the paragraph exists even if the response may misread it.
Fabricated citations are confined to legal cases, which is why the CPA.com toolkit's example is a court case.

feedback: OpenAI's page lists fabricated quotes, studies, citations, or references to non-existent sources among the forms a hallucination takes, and its practical advice is to always verify quotes, data, technical information, or references to external documents. A paragraph number is part of the citation, not evidence for it, so (a) mistakes the form of a claim for a check on it. Nothing in the sources says the model cites only what it has retrieved, and without search enabled the page says responses rest on training alone, so (c) has no support. The toolkit's court-case example is one example of a general failure, and OpenAI's definition of hallucination is not limited to any subject, so (d) narrows the failure in a way neither source does. Re-read section 02.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 3 (hallucination defined), entry 4 (fabricated citations named), entry 9 (always verify references) and entry 10 (without search, training only); file 4 entry 2 (the toolkit's court-case example, attributed); guide/03/02-hallucination.md, paragraphs 2 to 4. The section's one UNSOURCED flag (that a fabricated citation reads the same as a real one) is not what this question rests on.

stem: According to OpenAI's help page, what does the knowledge cutoff mean for a response, and what is the exception?

choices.text: Responses do not incorporate information about events after the point the training data runs to, unless tools such as search are used.
Responses include everything published up to the day of the question, because the model is retrained continuously.
The model refuses to answer about events after the cutoff, so a stale response cannot occur.
The cutoff applies only to numerical data; text sources are kept current.

feedback: The page lists the knowledge cutoff as a limitation: the models are trained on data up to a certain point, and responses do not incorporate information about events beyond that, unless tools are used. Both halves matter — the training data stops somewhere, and tools are the stated exception. The page also says that without search enabled, responses are based on what the model learned during training, which rules out (b). Nothing on the page says the model declines to answer past its cutoff; the risk the lesson calls staleness is exactly that it answers anyway, so (c) is the opposite of the point. The cutoff is stated for the training data as a whole, with no distinction between numbers and text, so (d) invents a limit the page does not draw. Re-read section 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 5 (knowledge cutoff; unless tools are used) and entry 10 (without search, training only); guide/03/03-knowledge-cutoff.md, first paragraph. No flag inherited — sec-03 carries no UNSOURCED flag.

stem: A response from ChatGPT is written in a firm, assured tone with no hedging. On the account given by OpenAI's help page and the CPA.com toolkit, what does that tone tell you about whether the response is correct?

choices.text: Nothing: the model may express high confidence even in incorrect answers, and a confident, articulate answer may mask that it is wrong.
It is evidence the response is correct, because the model hedges when its training data is thin.
It is evidence the response is wrong, because a correct response is usually hedged.
It shows the response came from a tool such as search, which is what makes it reliable.

feedback: OpenAI's page states it in three words, "Confidence isn't reliability", and explains that the model may express high confidence even in incorrect answers; the CPA.com toolkit says from the reader's side that confident, articulate and well-reasoned answers may mask the failing of getting things wrong. Tone, on both accounts, is not evidence either way. Choice (b) assumes the model signals thin training data by hedging, which no source says. Choice (c) makes the same mistake in reverse — the sources do not say confidence predicts error, only that it does not predict correctness. Choice (d) connects tone to tool use; the page says nothing of the kind, and section 05 says what does mark a computed answer. Re-read section 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 6 ("Confidence isn't reliability") and entry 2 (sound confident even when wrong); file 4 entry 1 (the toolkit on confident answers masking error, attributed); guide/03/04-confidence.md, first and second paragraphs. The section's UNSOURCED flag (tone in ordinary professional life) is the framing, not the answer, and this question does not rest on it.

stem: Which feature does OpenAI's help page tie accurate calculation to, and what does that mean for a number in an ordinary response?

choices.text: The tool the page prints as "Code interpreter / Data analysis", which it says enables accurate calculations; a number produced without it is generated text and is verified before it is relied on.
Search, which lets the model look the correct figure up on the web; without search, arithmetic is unreliable.
No feature is needed; the page says ChatGPT computes arithmetic reliably in every response.
Deep research, which the page says checks each calculation against several sources.

feedback: The page lists the tools ChatGPT may have access to, and the one it prints as "Code interpreter / Data analysis" is described as enabling accurate calculations, data visualizations, and structured logic. Accuracy is attached to that tool; of the ordinary response the page says only that it may be incorrect or misleading, and its practical advice is to always verify data. The page describes search as looking up current or niche information from the web and deep research as giving multi-source cited answers — neither is described as calculating, so (b) and (d) attach accuracy to the wrong tool. Choice (c) contradicts the page's opening statement about the ordinary response. Re-read section 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 12 (the tool enables accurate calculations), entry 1 (ordinary output may be incorrect or misleading) and entry 9 (always verify data); the tool's printed name and the search and deep research descriptions were read from the page's tools table (p. 2), per GPT-01 review J5; guide/03/05-calculation.md, second paragraph. The section's UNSOURCED flag (the one practical rule) is the synthesis this question's second half restates; the ruling of 2026-09-14 kept it.

stem: A colleague says that because ChatGPT is a computer program, a figure in its response has been calculated and can be relied on as arithmetic. Which reply is consistent with this lesson's sources?

choices.text: The response is produced from patterns in the training data, and the vendor says it can be incorrect or misleading; a figure in an ordinary response is generated, not computed.
The colleague is right: a language model is deterministic software, so its arithmetic is exact.
The colleague is right about arithmetic but not about text; the vendor's warning about incorrect output applies to prose only.
The figure can be relied on if the response states it confidently, because the model signals uncertainty when it is unsure.

feedback: OpenAI's page says ChatGPT provides responses based on patterns in the data it was trained on and, like any language model, can produce incorrect or misleading outputs; the CPA.com toolkit quotes an executive putting it as generated output, not computed answers, and adding that this is why you should not trust the models with math or financial analysis. Being software does not make the output a calculation, which is why (b) fails. The page's warning is about outputs generally and draws no line between numbers and prose, so (c) invents a distinction. Choice (d) is the confidence error: the page says the model may express high confidence even in incorrect answers. Re-read sections 01 and 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 1 (patterns; incorrect or misleading) and entry 6 (confidence); file 4 entry 3 ("generated output, not computed answers", a quoted executive, attributed); guide/03/01-generated-not-computed.md, paragraphs 2 and 4. No flag inherited.

stem: OpenAI's help page uses the word "hallucination". In the page's own definition, what does the term cover?

choices.text: Responses that are not factually accurate, including fabricated quotes, studies, citations, or references to sources that do not exist.
Only responses about events after the knowledge cutoff.
Only responses that sound uncertain; a confidently worded response is by definition not a hallucination.
Responses produced with search switched off; with search enabled, a hallucination cannot occur.

feedback: The page's definition is broad: a hallucination is when the model produces responses that are not factually accurate, and among the forms it names are fabricated quotes, studies, citations, or references to non-existent sources. The knowledge cutoff is listed separately as a limitation, not as the definition of hallucination, so (b) confuses two failures the lesson keeps apart. Choice (c) inverts the page, which says the model may sound confident even when it is wrong. Choice (d) attaches a guarantee to search that the page never gives — it says search lets the model cite web sources, not that it prevents inaccurate responses. Re-read sections 02 and 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 3 (hallucination defined), entry 4 (fabricated citations), entry 5 (knowledge cutoff, listed separately), entry 2 (sound confident even when wrong) and entry 10 (with search, cited web sources); guide/03/02-hallucination.md, first and second paragraphs. No flag inherited.

stem: A question put to ChatGPT turns on a figure that is revised every year, and no tool ran when the model answered. Which statement about the response follows from OpenAI's help page?

choices.text: The response is based on what the model learned during training, up to its knowledge cutoff, and the page's advice is to verify data before relying on it.
The response reflects the current figure, because the model checks the web whenever a question involves a date.
The response will state the cutoff date beside the figure, so the reader can tell whether it is current.
The response can be relied on as long as it is expressed with high confidence.

feedback: With no tool in use, the page says responses are based on what the model learned during training, and the knowledge cutoff means they do not incorporate information about events beyond the point the training data runs to. The page's own advice for that case is to always verify data. Choice (b) assumes a web check the page says happens only with search enabled. Choice (c) describes a disclosure no source says the model makes; this lesson gives no cutoff date for the same reason. Choice (d) is the confidence error again — high confidence is expressed even in incorrect answers. Re-read section 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 5 (knowledge cutoff), entry 10 (without search, training only), entry 9 (always verify data) and entry 6 (confidence); guide/03/03-knowledge-cutoff.md, first and last paragraphs. The stem's revised-every-year figure is sec-03's own hypothetical (GPT-01 review J2, accepted); it states no fact about any figure.

stem: A staff member pastes a schedule into ChatGPT and asks for the total, and the response gives a figure. Which of these is the position OpenAI's help page supports?

choices.text: The figure is generated text unless the code tool computed it; if it matters, it is recomputed or otherwise verified before it is relied on.
The figure is reliable because a total is simple arithmetic, which the language model performs exactly.
The figure is reliable if the response shows its working, since a calculation that is written out has been executed.
The figure cannot be relied on under any circumstances, because the page says ChatGPT cannot calculate.

feedback: The page attaches accurate calculation to the tool it prints as "Code interpreter / Data analysis"; of the ordinary response it says only that it may be incorrect or misleading, and it tells users to always verify data. A total is a number in a response like any other, so (b) is the mistake section 01 named — treating generated output as a computed answer. Written-out working is more generated text; nothing on the page says that showing steps means the tool ran, so (c) has no support. Choice (d) overstates the other way: the page says the tool enables accurate calculations, so a number the tool computed is exactly the case in which the model can calculate. Re-read section 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 12 (the tool enables accurate calculations), entry 1 (ordinary output may be incorrect or misleading) and entry 9 (always verify data); file 4 entry 3 (generated, not computed, attributed); guide/03/05-calculation.md, second and third paragraphs. The correct choice restates sec-05's UNSOURCED flag, the lesson's one practical rule, which the ruling of 2026-09-14 kept; its three components are the entries above.
